Collaborative documents

Many people edit the same document at the same moment and everyone must see a consistent result in a fraction of a second. Edits must never be lost, even if a server crashes in the middle of typing or two people type in the same place. Practise this hard system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

Many people edit the same document at the same moment and everyone must see a consistent result in a fraction of a second. Edits must never be lost, even if a server crashes in the middle of typing or two people type in the same place.

Think of shared docs like Google Docs.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
15 million people a month
Audience in plain numbers
15,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 40,000 requests per second
Request mix
Message: 60%; Sync change: 20%; Read: 15%; Write: 5%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Message: ≈ 250 ms; Sync change: ≈ 300 ms; Read: ≈ 300 ms; Write: ≈ 300 ms
Successful requests
99.95%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $83,000
Data at rest
≈ 60 TB
Where users are
North America: 50%; Europe: 50%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Message: 900 seconds; Sync change: 900 seconds; Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds
Fresh reads
People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.
Personal reads
90% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.
Required proofs
Managed encryption keys

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • 250,000 people editing at once, about a tenth typing in any one second (approx.).
  • One gateway node holds about 100,000 open connections (approx.).

Questions that shape the design

What if two people edit the same sentence together?

Both edits survive and everyone ends up with the same text. The order of edits is decided in one place per document.

How fast must an edit reach others?

Under about 250 ms, counting the trip across an ocean. More than that and cursors feel jumpy.

What if someone loses their connection?

They keep typing offline and their edits merge when they return.

Can we lose an edit?

Never. Typed text is saved before it is confirmed.

The traffic day

Traffic concentrated in working hours. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 09:00 · Synchronized rush

    Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

    Traffic for Read, Sync change, Message reaches 5 times the scheduled load; rises over 10 seconds, holds for 60 seconds and eases over 300 seconds. Other request types keep their scheduled load.

  2. 11:00 · Zone outage

    An availability zone loses power or network access.

    Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

  3. 14:30 · Network partition

    Your regions cannot talk to each other during the partition.

    Duration: ≈ 300 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Two people editing the same document must agree on the order. Where does that order get decided?
  • Converge concurrent edits and recover durable operations across reconnects.
  • One owner per document gives a clear order but is a single point to recover. The coordination service picks a new owner within seconds.
  • Writing to the log before confirming adds a few milliseconds but means no typed text is ever lost.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Related problems

  • Medium

    One-to-one chat

    People send short messages to each other from their phones. A message must arrive once, in order, even when the phone is on a bad connection and sends it again. If the other person is offline, the message waits and a notification goes out.

  • Medium

    File sync

    A folder on your laptop mirrors to the cloud and to your other devices. Small changes must arrive quickly, big files must upload reliably, and a shared folder with thousands of people must not melt the metadata service.

  • Hard

    Notes that sync across your devices

    Build a notebook that works on a phone and laptop, including a month offline. Edits should reach connected foreground devices in under a second, concurrent work must not disappear, and the server should not need plaintext notes. Push wakes devices; durable sync must work when push does not.

  • Hard

    Scheduled job service

    Customers register jobs: "call my web address every night at 02:00" or "every hour on the hour". Aim to fire within 5 seconds; work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed. Retry safely after a crash. One external effect requires the customer endpoint to honor a stable job occurrence key. Half the world picks the top of the hour, so a huge crowd of jobs comes due in the same second.
